title: Palpitations: Capture the Rhythm and Find the Risk
bottomLine: Palpitations are a symptom, not a rhythm diagnosis. Determine whether there is hemodynamic risk, obtain ECG/rhythm correlation, identify triggers and structural disease, and choose ambulatory monitoring based on event frequency rather than ordering the same monitor for everyone.
recognize: Abrupt regular rapid palpitations suggest re-entrant SVT; irregular palpitations may reflect AF or ectopy; skipped beats often reflect premature beats.
Syncope, exertional symptoms, chest pain, HF or family history sudden death make palpitations higher risk.
differentiate: Anxiety, hyperthyroidism, anemia, stimulant/caffeine use, pregnancy and medications can mimic or provoke arrhythmia symptoms.
Sinus tachycardia has an underlying driver and should not be treated like an isolated re-entrant arrhythmia before the cause is addressed.
assessment: Ask onset/offset, regularity, duration, triggers, exertional relationship, syncope/presyncope, chest pain, dyspnea, medications/substances and family history.
Assess vitals, cardiac exam and orthostatic status when relevant.
workup: Obtain 12-lead ECG and use CBC/electrolytes/TSH or pregnancy testing when clinically indicated.
Use Holter, patch or event monitoring matched to symptom frequency and suspected arrhythmia burden.
management: Treat the documented arrhythmia and reversible trigger; refer symptomatic recurrent SVT, AF, ventricular arrhythmia or structural-heart-disease concern to cardiology/electrophysiology.
Unstable tachy/bradyarrhythmia requires acute-care management.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric rate-slowing drugs before identifying the rhythm when pre-excitation, bradycardia or another contraindication is plausible.
counselling: Teach symptom/rhythm documentation and when to seek emergency care rather than repeatedly checking pulse without a plan.
followUp: Review monitor results and close the loop on cardiology referral or medication changes.
examTrap: Treating palpitations as anxiety before obtaining basic rhythm assessment in a patient with syncope or exertional symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Palpitations become a diagnosis only when the rhythm and context are captured.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Heart Rhythm Society arrhythmia resources

title: Anticoagulation and Reversal: Drug, Last Dose, Renal Function, Bleeding Severity
bottomLine: Anticoagulant bleeding management depends on the drug, timing of last dose, renal/hepatic function, bleeding site/severity and whether urgent surgery is required. Stop life-threatening bleeding first, use the correct reversal strategy, and remember that routine PT/aPTT cannot reliably exclude clinically important DOAC effect.
recognize: Major bleeding is defined by clinical consequences—hemodynamic compromise, critical-site bleeding or meaningful hemoglobin loss/transfusion need—not by bruising alone.
Drug clearance and reversal needs differ for warfarin, dabigatran, factor-Xa inhibitors and heparins.
differentiate: Minor bleeding may need local measures and dose review rather than reversal; life-threatening bleeding requires urgent hemostatic action.
INR guides warfarin effect but is not a quantitative DOAC monitor.
assessment: Confirm drug, dose, last dose, indication, renal/hepatic function, concurrent antiplatelets/NSAIDs, bleeding site and hemodynamics.
Assess thrombotic risk created by stopping/reversing therapy as part of the restart plan.
workup: Use CBC, platelets, creatinine, liver tests, type/screen and coagulation tests as appropriate; use drug-specific assays when available and management-relevant.
A normal routine PT/aPTT does not reliably rule out clinically significant factor-Xa inhibitor effect.
management: Warfarin emergency reversal uses IV vitamin K plus 4-factor PCC according to current Canadian guidance.

Dabigatran severe bleeding can use idarucizumab; apixaban/rivaroxaban life-threatening/uncontrolled bleeding may use andexanet alfa where available/indicated, with PCC as a nonspecific alternative in selected settings.
UFH can be reversed with protamine; LMWH reversal is incomplete and specialist/protocol guided.
medicationSafety: Reversal agents and PCC carry thrombotic risk; use them when bleeding risk outweighs that harm.
Restart anticoagulation only after bleeding control and re-evaluation of indication/timing.
redFlags: Emergency surgery with active anticoagulant effect
counselling: Teach patients to report major bleeding, head injury and interacting OTC medications and to carry an accurate anticoagulant list.
followUp: Document the reversal/restart plan and reassess renal function, indication and interacting drugs after the event.
examTrap: Using a normal INR to declare apixaban inactive—or reversing every minor bleed without considering thrombotic risk.
oneLinePearl: Reversal starts with four facts: drug, last dose, clearance, and bleeding severity.

title: Cardiomyopathy: Define the Phenotype Before Calling It Heart Failure
bottomLine: Cardiomyopathy is myocardial disease with multiple phenotypes and causes. Define dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive/infiltrative or arrhythmogenic features, exclude ischemic/valvular/pressure-load causes, and identify inherited or sudden-death risk that changes family screening and referral.
recognize: Dilated disease may present with HFrEF/arrhythmia; hypertrophic disease may cause exertional dyspnea, chest pain or syncope; infiltrative disease may produce restrictive physiology and conduction disease.
Family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden death is a major diagnostic clue.
differentiate: Ischemic, valvular and longstanding hypertensive disease can cause ventricular dysfunction but should not be mislabeled primary cardiomyopathy without evaluation.
Athlete's-heart remodeling differs from pathologic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and may require expert assessment.
assessment: Assess HF symptoms, syncope, palpitations, pregnancy/peripartum timing, toxins/alcohol, chemotherapy, viral illness, systemic disease and three-generation family history when inherited disease is possible.
workup: Use ECG and echocardiography as core testing, with coronary evaluation, CMR, genetic testing or biopsy selected by phenotype and specialist indication.
Evaluate reversible endocrine/toxic/inflammatory causes when the history suggests them.
management: Treat HF/arrhythmias according to phenotype and guideline-directed therapy; restrict disease-specific high-risk activity when indicated.
Refer suspected inherited, hypertrophic, infiltrative/arrhythmogenic or rapidly progressive disease to cardiology/genetics and address family screening.
medicationSafety: Avoid therapies that worsen preload/outflow obstruction or conduction disease in susceptible phenotypes without specialist guidance.
Pregnancy/peripartum cardiomyopathy requires pregnancy-specific medication selection.
counselling: Discuss family implications and genetic counseling when inherited disease is suspected.
followUp: Track ventricular function, rhythm and symptoms and ensure family/specialist evaluation is completed.
examTrap: Calling every reduced EF idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy before excluding ischemic, valvular, toxic and genetic causes.
oneLinePearl: Cardiomyopathy is a phenotype-and-cause diagnosis, not another word for low EF.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society heart-failure/cardiomyopathy practice resources

title: Pericarditis and Myocarditis: Chest Pain, Inflammation, Arrhythmia, and Hemodynamic Risk
bottomLine: Pericarditis and myocarditis can mimic ACS. Distinguish pericardial inflammation from myocardial injury, rule out coronary disease when appropriate, and escalate tamponade, ventricular dysfunction, high-grade conduction disease or malignant arrhythmia.
recognize: Pericarditis often causes pleuritic positional chest pain, diffuse ST/PR changes or effusion; myocarditis may cause chest pain, troponin rise, HF or arrhythmia after infection/inflammation.
Normal troponin does not exclude myocarditis.
differentiate: Regional ischemic ECG changes/coronary-pattern symptoms favour ACS; PE and aortic disease remain alternate chest-pain emergencies.
Pericardial effusion is not tamponade unless hemodynamics are compromised.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, JVP, heart sounds, HF signs, arrhythmia, recent infection/vaccination/systemic inflammation, medications and exertional symptoms.
workup: Use ECG, troponin, natriuretic peptide, inflammatory markers and echocardiography as indicated; CMR can support myocarditis diagnosis.
Endomyocardial biopsy is reserved for selected severe/uncertain cases at experienced centres.
management: Treat uncomplicated pericarditis according to anti-inflammatory guidance after contraindication review.
Myocarditis management focuses on HF/arrhythmia support and activity restriction with expert follow-up; routine antiviral therapy is not recommended.
Tamponade, shock, severe ventricular dysfunction or malignant arrhythmia requires urgent hospital/specialty care.
medicationSafety: Avoid exercise during active myocarditis because arrhythmia/sudden-death risk is increased.
Immunosuppression for myocarditis should be specialist/etiology guided rather than empiric.
counselling: Explain activity restriction and the need for follow-up until myocarditis resolves or a chronic plan is established.
followUp: Repeat cardiac assessment based on symptoms/function and ensure specialist clearance before return to intense exercise.
examTrap: Calling elevated troponin myocarditis without excluding ACS—or calling an effusion tamponade without hemodynamic compromise.
oneLinePearl: Pericarditis inflames the sac; myocarditis injures the muscle and raises arrhythmia/HF risk.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society heart-failure myocarditis guidance

title: Aortic Stenosis: Symptoms, Severity, Ventricular Response, and Timely Valve Referral
bottomLine: Aortic stenosis becomes dangerous when severe disease is symptomatic or ventricular response deteriorates. Exertional dyspnea, angina or syncope with significant AS requires prompt structural-heart assessment; murmur intensity alone does not determine severity.
recognize: Classic symptoms are exertional dyspnea, angina and syncope; older adults may report reduced activity instead.
Late-peaking systolic murmur, diminished carotid upstroke and LV hypertrophy support the diagnosis but echo defines severity.
differentiate: Low-flow states can produce severe AS with a softer murmur/discordant gradients.
Syncope can have arrhythmic/orthostatic causes even when AS is present; evaluate the whole event.
assessment: Assess exertional symptoms, presyncope/syncope, HF, functional decline, BP, rhythm, frailty and goals of care.
workup: Use echocardiography for valve area/velocity/gradient and ventricular function; stress or advanced imaging is selected by cardiology when symptoms/severity are discordant.
management: Refer severe symptomatic AS and other guideline-supported intervention candidates to a multidisciplinary valve team for TAVR/SAVR evaluation.
Manage HF/AF carefully while awaiting intervention and avoid delaying referral for repeated routine follow-up once symptoms emerge.
medicationSafety: Aggressive vasodilation/diuresis can cause hypotension in severe fixed obstruction and should be individualized.
There is no medication that reverses severe calcific valve obstruction.
counselling: Teach patients to report new exertional symptoms immediately and discuss driving/activity implications after syncope.
followUp: Use guideline-directed echo surveillance for asymptomatic disease and prompt valve-team referral when intervention criteria appear.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with severe AS because the murmur is soft or because symptoms are attributed to age/deconditioning.
oneLinePearl: In aortic stenosis, symptoms change the clock.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society valvular/Drive & Fly resources

title: Mitral Valve Prolapse: Define Regurgitation and Arrhythmic Risk, Not Just the Click
bottomLine: Mitral valve prolapse is often benign, but the clinically important questions are whether significant mitral regurgitation, ventricular remodeling or arrhythmia is present. Use echocardiographic severity and symptoms—not an auscultatory click alone—to guide follow-up/referral.
recognize: MVP may cause a midsystolic click/late systolic murmur and can be asymptomatic.
Progressive MR can cause dyspnea, AF or HF; selected patients have ventricular ectopy/arrhythmic risk.
differentiate: Palpitations/anxiety symptoms do not prove arrhythmic MVP.
A benign click without significant MR differs from flail leaflet/severe MR.
assessment: Assess exertional dyspnea, palpitations/syncope, family history sudden death, connective-tissue disease and prior echo findings.
workup: Use echocardiography to assess leaflet morphology, MR severity and chamber response; use ambulatory rhythm monitoring for meaningful palpitations/syncope.
management: Observe mild/asymptomatic disease with appropriate surveillance.
Refer significant MR, progressive chamber changes, arrhythmia or symptoms to cardiology/valve team.
medicationSafety: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated solely for MVP.
Treat AF/arrhythmia according to the documented rhythm and stroke risk rather than the valve label alone.
counselling: Reassure low-risk patients while explaining which symptoms warrant earlier reassessment.
followUp: Echo interval depends on MR severity and ventricular response; review sooner if symptoms change.
examTrap: Giving dental antibiotic prophylaxis solely because a patient has MVP.
oneLinePearl: MVP risk comes from regurgitation and rhythm, not the click itself.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society valvular-heart-disease practice resources

title: Severe Blood Pressure: Emergency Means Acute Organ Injury
bottomLine: Hypertensive emergency is severe BP elevation with acute target-organ injury—not a number alone. Repeat the measurement correctly, search for neurologic/cardiac/aortic/renal/retinal/pregnancy injury, and avoid rapid IV normalization in an otherwise asymptomatic patient without acute injury.
recognize: Focal deficit, encephalopathy, acute pulmonary edema, ACS, aortic syndrome, AKI, visual injury or pregnancy severe features make the situation emergent.
Pain, anxiety, medication nonadherence and measurement error can produce very high readings without emergency organ injury.
differentiate: Severe asymptomatic hypertension usually needs confirmation, medication review and timely oral/outpatient management rather than immediate IV lowering.
Preeclampsia/postpartum severe hypertension follows obstetric emergency pathways.
assessment: Repeat BP with correct technique/cuff and assess mental status, focal neurology, cardiopulmonary status, volume, pulses/aortic symptoms and pregnancy/postpartum status.
workup: Use ECG/troponin, creatinine/electrolytes/urinalysis, imaging and fundoscopy only as targeted by suspected organ injury.
management: Emergency organ injury requires ED/hospital controlled BP reduction using syndrome-specific IV therapy.
Without acute injury, address triggers, restart/intensify appropriate oral treatment and arrange close follow-up; avoid precipitous reduction.
medicationSafety: Overly rapid BP reduction can cause cerebral/coronary/renal hypoperfusion.
counselling: Explain the difference between a dangerous BP complication and a high reading that still needs long-term treatment.
followUp: For outpatient severe asymptomatic hypertension, arrange prompt reassessment and access/adherence review.
examTrap: Choosing rapid normalization of an asymptomatic high reading instead of assessing for target-organ injury.
oneLinePearl: Hypertensive emergency is defined by the injured organ, not the frightening number.

title: Cardiac Biomarkers: Myocardial Injury, Heart-Failure Probability, and Clinical Context
bottomLine: Troponin above the assay reference indicates myocardial injury, not automatically MI; MI requires an ischemic clinical context. BNP/NT-proBNP changes HF probability but is influenced by age, AF, renal function and obesity. Serial trends and the patient matter more than one number.
recognize: Troponin can rise in ACS, myocarditis, PE, sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, HF and renal disease.
Natriuretic peptides rise with myocardial wall stress and can support HF diagnosis/risk assessment.
differentiate: Acute MI requires rise/fall in troponin plus ischemic evidence; chronic stable elevation is different.
CK-MB adds little when high-sensitivity troponin is available for modern ACS evaluation.
assessment: Interpret symptoms, ECG, hemodynamics, renal function, arrhythmia and timing from symptom onset alongside biomarker values.
workup: Use serial high-sensitivity troponin in a validated local algorithm; use BNP/NT-proBNP when it changes HF probability/management.
Do not order serial biomarkers without a clinical question.
management: Treat the underlying syndrome—ACS, HF, PE, sepsis, myocarditis—not the biomarker number.
Escalate dynamic ischemia, shock, acute HF or arrhythmia despite modest biomarker levels.
medicationSafety: Do not start antithrombotics solely from an elevated troponin without evaluating the ischemic diagnosis/bleeding risk.
redFlags: Rapid troponin rise with ischemic symptoms
counselling: Explain that a troponin can be abnormal for several reasons and requires interpretation with the heart rhythm/ECG/symptoms.
followUp: Ensure the cause of myocardial injury and any HF biomarker elevation is documented and managed.
examTrap: Calling any elevated troponin NSTEMI or using BNP alone to diagnose HF.
oneLinePearl: Troponin tells you myocardium was injured; the clinical story tells you why.

title: Advanced ECG Interpretation: Rate, Rhythm, Axis, Intervals, Ischemia, and Immediate Risk
bottomLine: Advanced ECG interpretation is systematic: confirm calibration/quality, determine rate/rhythm, P-QRS relationship, axis, intervals/QRS morphology and ST-T pattern, then identify findings that demand immediate action. The ECG must be interpreted with symptoms and prior tracings.
recognize: Wide-complex tachycardia should be presumed ventricular until appropriately evaluated.
High-grade AV block, pre-excitation, long QT, acute ischemic changes and hyperkalemic patterns are clinically high risk.
differentiate: Early repolarization/pericarditis can mimic STEMI; bundle branch block/pacing complicates ischemia interpretation.
Artifact can mimic arrhythmia—check the patient/pulse.
assessment: Always connect ECG to hemodynamics, chest pain, syncope, electrolyte/drug exposure and prior rhythm history.
workup: Compare previous ECG, repeat with evolving symptoms and use electrolytes/troponin/imaging according to the suspected syndrome.
management: Treat unstable rhythm/ischemia using acute-care algorithms and seek expert interpretation when complex conduction/ischemia patterns exceed local scope.
Do not delay emergency treatment while pursuing perfect ECG classification in an unstable patient.
medicationSafety: QT-prolonging and AV-nodal drugs require interval/conduction context; correct electrolytes when arrhythmia risk is present.
counselling: Explain when an ECG finding requires emergency assessment versus outpatient monitoring.
followUp: Arrange rhythm/cardiology follow-up for significant incidental conduction or arrhythmic abnormalities.
examTrap: Treating a monitor label as the rhythm diagnosis without reading the actual ECG and patient pulse.
oneLinePearl: Read every ECG in the same order, then ask which finding changes the next action.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Heart Rhythm Society arrhythmia resources

title: Cardiac Stress Testing: Choose the Test the Patient Can Answer
bottomLine: Stress-test selection depends on the clinical question, ability to exercise, baseline ECG interpretability, pretest probability and comorbidity. A positive or negative result changes probability; it does not override an unstable presentation or a poor-quality/nondiagnostic study.
recognize: Exercise ECG is most useful when the patient can exercise adequately and baseline ECG permits ischemia interpretation.
Stress imaging is favored when baseline ECG is uninterpretable, exercise is limited or imaging adds risk/localization information.
differentiate: Stress testing is for stable diagnostic/risk questions, not active ACS or unstable symptoms.
A nondiagnostic test is not a negative test.
assessment: Assess symptom stability, exercise capacity, baseline ECG, known CAD, asthma/COPD, conduction disease, pregnancy and medication effects.
workup: Select exercise ECG, stress echo, nuclear or other functional/anatomic testing based on the patient and local pathways.
Interpret result with pretest probability and achieved workload/heart rate/quality.
management: Refer high-risk ischemia or persistent symptoms for cardiology/anatomic evaluation.
Do not repeat low-value testing in asymptomatic low-risk patients without a management question.
medicationSafety: Pharmacologic stress agents have bronchospasm, hypotension, conduction and arrhythmia considerations; follow test-specific contraindications.
redFlags: Poor exercise tolerance with concerning symptoms
counselling: Explain why a test may be nondiagnostic and why symptoms can still require reassessment despite a prior negative study.
followUp: Close the loop on abnormal/nondiagnostic tests and avoid repeated testing without a new clinical question.
examTrap: Ordering an exercise treadmill test in a patient with active unstable chest pain or an uninterpretable baseline ECG without considering a better modality.
oneLinePearl: Stress testing is only as useful as the question, patient, and test quality.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society chronic coronary/testing practice resources
